newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends higher after roller-coaster day.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends higher after roller-coaster day.

text.p: NYMEX crude oil prices closed higher Thursday as fears of bullish overnight news on the Iraqi conflict sparked a late session rally following a day of big price swings, traders said.
"You have players not wanting to go home short which creates late bidding," said Thomas Blakeslee of Cargill Investor Services.
October crude closed up 25 cents at $25.00 a barrel after rising as high as $25.30 and falling as low as $24.26.
"It was a roller-coaster day, and everybody's waiting to see what's going to go on with Iraq," said a trader.

The United States said it was readying F-117A stealth bombers and B-52 long-range bombers in retaliation against Iraq after Iraq fired missiles at U.S. jets. Iraq warned Kuwait not to permit U.S. planes to use it as an attack base.
Meanwhile, October heating oil led price gains, rising 0.98 cent to 69.17 cent a gallon. Heat followed strong gains by gas oil futures on London's IPE made on supply concerns.
"Heating oil's fundamentals remain the strongest with ongoing supply concerns," said Cargill's Blakeslee.
October gasoline ended the day unchanged at 65.91 cents a gallon.
Traders said gasoline prices drifted on relatively low volume as the summer travel season has made gasoline the least compelling leg of the oil complex.
However, dealers said the gasoline-to-crude crack spread had narrowed to one of the lowest levels since reformulated gasoline began trading on the NYMEX, and was making gasoline's price attractive.
At Thursday's close the October gasoline-to-crude crack spread had narrowed to $2.68 a barrel from $2.93 a barrel Wednesday.
October crude's closing price Thursday was the highest closing price for crude since the end of 1991.
After the market's close Kuwait, one of the 11 OPEC members, rejected Iraq's warning against allowing U.S. planes to use its bases for military strikes.
Some traders said crude's price is overblown since the Iraqi conflict has yet to disrupt oil output from the Middle East region, the key supplier of the world's oil.
"For crude to close at $25.00, the market probably needs to believe that Iraq may attack Kuwait," said Cargill's Blakeslee.
Traders said the price effect of Friday's options expiry for October crude was muted due to the Iraqi situation.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
